title: FAST-PETase, a machine-learning-engineered enzyme, depolymerized post-consumer PET and was reused by an independent lab
summary: A neural network helped researchers develop FAST-PETase, which degraded 51 PET products in laboratory tests. A separate group later used it with MHETase to produce monomers from PET film.
account: In a Nature paper of 27 April 2022, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin used a structure-based machine-learning algorithm. The algorithm, an ensemble of three three-dimensional convolutional neural networks, selected stabilizing mutations in a polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolase, producing FAST-PETase. They reported that untreated post-consumer PET from 51 different thermoformed products was almost completely degraded within one week at 50 degrees Celsius. The enzyme outperformed wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 degrees Celsius. They closed the loop by resynthesizing PET from the recovered monomers. An independent group at Texas A&M University used FAST-PETase together with MHETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst (Environmental Science and Technology Letters, 19 March 2025). The later yeast system produced 4.95 mM terephthalic acid from PET film after seven days at 30 degrees Celsius, with no accumulation of MHET intermediates. This result does not establish that the entire starting film was degraded.
purpose: Use a structure-based machine-learning model to predict stabilizing mutations that make a PET hydrolase active and robust at moderate temperatures.
system: Structure-based machine-learning mutation predictor (ensemble of three 3D convolutional neural networks) applied to PETase engineering
developer: University of Texas at Austin (Alper and Ellington groups)
deployer: University of Texas at Austin; subsequently Texas A&M University

ratings.reason: A laboratory-scale enzyme that an independent group could pick up and reuse successfully; the sources report bench work, not production deployment.
Complete depolymerization of untreated post-consumer PET was shown only in the laboratory in both the original and the independent study. Neither source reports industrial-scale recycling.

comparator.against: wild-type PETase and previously engineered PET hydrolases
comparator.after: superior PET-hydrolytic activity relative to both wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 °C and a range of pH levels
comparator.quote: Our mutant and scaffold combination (FAST-PETase: functional, active, stable and tolerant PETase) contains five mutations compared to wild-type PETase (N233K/R224Q/S121E from prediction and D186H/R280A from scaffold) and shows superior PET-hydrolytic activity relative to both wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 °C and a range of pH levels.

later.note: An independent Texas A&M group adopted FAST-PETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst and reported complete depolymerization of a PET film in seven days.
later.quote: Co-immobilization of FAST-PETase and MHETase on a surface-displayed trifunctional scaffoldin led to complete depolymerization of PET into its constituent monomers TPA and EG, with no accumulation of reaction intermediates. In our system, the presence of MHETase along with FAST-PETase led to a nearly 5-fold boost in product formation, and attachment of FAST-PETase at two sites on the trifunctional scaffoldin further boosted yields by up to 1.8-fold. TPA yields of 4.95 mM were obtained in 7 days on an amorphous PET film with no pretreatment requirement.

fields.account: In a Nature paper of 27 April 2022, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin used a structure-based machine-learning algorithm. The algorithm, an ensemble of three three-dimensional convolutional neural networks, selected stabilizing mutations in a polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolase, producing FAST-PETase. They reported that untreated post-consumer PET from 51 different thermoformed products was almost completely degraded within one week at 50 degrees Celsius. The enzyme outperformed wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 degrees Celsius. They closed the loop by resynthesizing PET from the recovered monomers. An independent group at Texas A&M University used FAST-PETase together with MHETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst (Environmental Science and Technology Letters, 19 March 2025). The later yeast system produced 4.95 mM terephthalic acid from PET film after seven days at 30 degrees Celsius, with no accumulation of MHET intermediates. This result does not establish that the entire starting film was degraded.
